findings.title: Admin API errors converted to null after logging, no propagation
findings.note: Cause is preserved via console.error(e), so this is not a silent swallow, but the exception is still converted to a null return value with no re-throw or error signal, making it indistinguishable from a valid empty admin response to any caller.
findings.proof: Confirmed mechanically: catch block (lines 14-17) logs via console.error(e) then returns null instead of rethrowing, so a caller cannot distinguish failure from a legitimately empty/null JSON response. However, grep across the repo shows getAdminJson has zero in-repo callers, so no code path is actually misled today — this is latent risk in currently-dead code rather than an active masking bug affecting a real caller.
checked: cause preservation in catch (console.error(e) — preserved for logs only)

findings.title: Empty catch block silently swallows all fetch/JSON errors
findings.note: Network errors, non-JSON responses, and thrown auth/timeout failures are caught and discarded with no logging; the function falls through to return null, indistinguishable from a legitimate empty response. No caller in the repo currently consumes getJson, so the failure is invisible to everyone.
findings.proof: client.ts:11 `catch (e) {}` discards network errors, non-JSON bodies, and abort errors with no logging, falling through to return null (line 15), indistinguishable from a valid empty response. client-admin.ts:14-17 logs the error via console.error before returning null, showing the intended pattern. Grep across src/ finds no caller of getJson anywhere in the repo (only its own definition), so the masking is currently latent rather than actively hiding a live failure today, but the code itself is a real error-masking defect for any future/external caller.
checked: rethrow/cause preservation: none, error is dropped

findings.title: Coverage threshold configured but never enforced by test run
findings.note: jest's coverageThreshold only fails a run under --coverage; both the 'test' script and CI invoke plain jest, so the 80% gate is dead config and CI cannot fail on the untested hotspot files above.

evidence.quote: "scripts": { "build": "tsc -p tsconfig.json", "test": "jest" },
"jest": { "coverageThreshold": { "global": { "lines": 80 } } }
command: npm test

findings.proof: package.json:8 sets jest coverageThreshold to 80% lines, but package.json:5's test script is plain `jest` with no --coverage flag, and ci.yml:19 invokes `npm test` (same plain script). Jest only enforces coverageThreshold when run with --coverage, so this gate never executes and cannot fail a build regardless of actual coverage.

findings.title: CI wraps the whole test run in a 3-attempt retry
findings.note: The entire npm test invocation, not an individual flaky test, is retried up to 3 times; this configuration would silently absorb any non-deterministic test failure without surfacing it, though no flaky-commit history was available to confirm one exists.

evidence.quote:
- uses: nick-fields/retry@7152eba30c6575329ac0576536151aca5a72780e
        with:
          timeout_minutes: 10
          max_attempts: 3
          command: npm test

findings.proof: ci.yml:15-19 wraps the bare `npm test` command (not npm install) in nick-fields/retry with max_attempts: 3. Any single test run that fails non-deterministically gets up to two silent re-runs before the job is marked failed, and CI never surfaces that a retry occurred. This applies to the whole suite, not a scoped flaky test, so genuine intermittent failures are indistinguishable from a clean pass in the workflow's final status.
checked: retry scope (whole command vs single test)

findings.title: Cart total test asserts against opaque magic number
findings.note: Assertion is a bare literal (2000) with no derivation from the unit price or quantity used in the test, so a reader cannot tell if the expectation is correct without cross-referencing pricing.ts separately.
findings.proof: cart.test.ts:6 asserts total(cart)===2000 with no visible derivation. Tracing the callees: cart.ts:17 computes sum of priceOf(sku)*qty, and pricing.ts:3 sets A1's price to 1000; with qty:2 (test line 5) the correct expected value is 1000*2=2000, so the assertion is numerically correct, but a reader must open two other files to confirm that — the literal is opaque in isolation as described.
